objectives.text: Distinguish canon, institutional teaching, commentary, and historical evidence.
State a doctrinal claim with a source and a limit.

sources.title: Approaching Latter-day Saint Doctrine
sources.editorialNote: Institutional guidance on identifying doctrine; an interpretive guide, not a complete hierarchy of every statement.

sources.title: Sources, authority, and careful claims
sources.body: Studying doctrine begins with identifying the kind of claim being made. A passage can be canonical, a statement can represent current institutional teaching, and a book can offer useful commentary without all three having the same function. A historical record may tell us what someone taught at a particular time without settling what the Church teaches today. Keep four fields beside every note: claim, source, setting, and confidence. Ask whether your wording is broader than the evidence. “This passage teaches…” is often more defensible than “Every Latter-day Saint believes…”. This course assesses your ability to understand and explain teachings; it does not assess personal belief or religious worthiness. Start a source ledger now. You will revise it as new evidence changes how precisely you can express a claim.

questions.prompt: Which collection consists of the four Latter-day Saint standard works?

options.text: Bible, Book of Mormon, Doctrine and Covenants, Pearl of Great Price
Bible, Book of Mormon, general conference addresses, Church History
Old Testament, New Testament, Book of Mormon, Doctrine and Covenants
Bible, Articles of Faith, Church Handbook, Pearl of Great Price

questions.explanation: The institutional guide names these four works. Conference addresses and the handbook are not additional standard works; the Old and New Testaments belong to the Bible.

sourceLocators.locator: Principles on isolated statements, context, standard works, and future change

questions.prompt: A single author offers a new explanation in a devotional book, and you have not found institutional endorsement. How should you provisionally classify the explanation?

options.text: Canonical text
Official declaration
Individual commentary
Historical consensus

questions.explanation: A proposal in a devotional book is commentary. Canonical or institutional status requires additional evidence; popularity does not establish consensus.

sourceLocators.locator: Principles on isolated statements, context, standard works, and future change

questions.prompt: A diary records what a Church member taught in 1880. Which claim does that entry most directly support?

options.text: The teaching is binding on members today
The diarist reports this teaching in that setting
The teaching was widely discussed in that ward
The teaching was included in the standard works

questions.explanation: The entry directly establishes what the diarist reports. Broader claims about present authority, wider discussion, or canonization need further evidence.
questions.perspective: Original Hearken reading method grounded in the cited sources

questions.prompt: According to the Church’s guide to approaching doctrine, how should an isolated statement by a leader be treated?

options.text: As binding whenever the speaker held a leadership office
As sufficient if it appeared in print
As doctrine if it has been widely quoted
As a statement whose context and doctrinal standing need examination

questions.explanation: The guide cautions that a single statement on one occasion does not necessarily constitute binding doctrine. Office, publication, and circulation alone do not settle its status.

sourceLocators.locator: Principles on isolated statements, context, standard works, and future change

questions.prompt: Which revision best matches the evidence when your source is one institutional explanation?

options.text: This explanation teaches the claim; it does not establish every member’s personal view.
Most members believe the claim because an institutional explanation exists.
This explanation establishes how the claim has always been taught.
This explanation is the only possible interpretation of the canonical texts.

questions.explanation: Attribution limits the claim to the source consulted. The other answers infer member opinions, historical continuity, or exclusive interpretation without evidence.
questions.perspective: Original Hearken reading method grounded in the cited sources

questions.prompt: A note quotes Article of Faith 4’s list of first principles and ordinances. Which source category applies to the quoted passage?

options.text: Historical diary
Individual commentary
Canonical text
Institutional handbook

questions.explanation: The quoted passage belongs to the Articles of Faith in the Pearl of Great Price, a standard work. A reader’s explanation of it may be commentary, but the question asks about the passage itself.

questions.prompt: An 1880 diary and a current institutional explanation use different wording about the same topic. Which source-ledger decision best preserves the available evidence?

options.text: Mark the diary as describing the current teaching
Record the date, setting, and claim of each source before explaining the difference
Merge the two accounts into a single statement without dates
Mark the current explanation as confirming every detail in the diary

questions.explanation: Separate dated records preserve the evidence for later comparison. The other options assume continuity or agreement without examining the actual claims.
questions.perspective: Original Hearken reading method grounded in the cited sources

questions.prompt: Which statement both attributes Article of Faith 2 accurately and stays within its claim?

options.text: Article of Faith 2 explains every consequence of the Fall
Article of Faith 2 establishes how every Christian tradition understands original sin
Article of Faith 2 says human choices have no consequences
Article of Faith 2 assigns punishment for personal sins rather than Adam’s transgression

questions.explanation: The fourth statement accurately attributes the article’s specific claim. The others extend it into an exhaustive account, a universal Christian position, or a denial of responsibility.

questions.prompt: The Church’s guide to doctrine allows for future additions or changes to teachings or practices.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: The guide describes the Church’s teachings and practices as open to future revelation and change.

questions.prompt: A devotional commentary becomes canonical simply because it quotes an Article of Faith.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: The canonical status of a quoted passage does not automatically extend to the commentary quoting it.
